This node bundles four genuinely separate costs of inflation (menu costs, shoe-leather costs, redistributive effects, uncertainty/investment costs) into one node's essentialPoints, violating the one-idea-per-node rule and the ~4-item ceiling border; each is independently examinable and should be split.

new_nodes.label: Menu costs of inflation
new_nodes.objective: Understand menu costs as the resource cost of repricing under inflation.
essentialPoints: Firms incur costs of repricing goods (physical menus, catalogues, systems) under inflation

new_nodes.label: Shoe-leather costs of inflation
new_nodes.objective: Understand shoe-leather costs as the cost of economising on money holdings under inflation.
essentialPoints: Higher inflation raises opportunity cost of holding money, prompting more frequent bank/ATM visits

new_nodes.label: Redistributive effects of unexpected inflation
new_nodes.objective: Understand how unexpected inflation redistributes real wealth between creditors and debtors.
essentialPoints: Unexpected inflation erodes the real value of fixed nominal debts, benefiting debtors at creditors' expense

new_nodes.label: Inflation uncertainty and investment costs
new_nodes.objective: Understand how inflation uncertainty discourages investment and long-term planning.
essentialPoints: Uncertain future price levels raise risk premia and discourage long-term contracts and investment

issues.explanation: This node bundles two independently markable efficiency properties (allocative efficiency P=MC and productive efficiency at minimum ATC) into one node; a mark scheme would credit these separately per rule 15.

new_nodes.label: Allocative efficiency of perfect competition
new_nodes.objective: Evaluate why P=MC in perfect competition implies allocative efficiency.
essentialPoints: Price equals marginal cost in long-run competitive equilibrium
This means resources are allocated to their highest-valued use, maximising total surplus
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - consumer/producer welfare

new_nodes.label: Productive efficiency of perfect competition
new_nodes.objective: Evaluate why competitive firms produce at minimum average total cost in the long run.
essentialPoints: Long-run equilibrium forces firms to produce at minimum LRAC
This means goods are produced using the fewest possible resources
specRefs: EC109 syllabus: Perfect Competition - consumer/producer welfare

issues.explanation: This adv/dis set has only one advantages node and one disadvantages node bundling multiple distinct points each; per the breadth check, a real mark scheme credits 4-6 distinct points, and the advantages node itself bundles 'immediate/direct AD increase', 'can be targeted', and 'multiplier effect' as one node, and the disadvantages node bundles four distinct drawbacks (lags, crowding out, debt, political constraints) as one node.

new_nodes.label: Fiscal policy directly and immediately raises aggregate demand
new_nodes.objective: Understand that government purchases enter AD directly without needing to alter private behaviour first.
essentialPoints: Government spending is itself a component of AD, so a rise in G directly and immediately increases demand

new_nodes.label: Fiscal policy can be targeted at specific sectors/groups
new_nodes.objective: Understand the precision advantage of fiscal policy over economy-wide tools.
essentialPoints: Spending and tax changes can be aimed at particular regions, sectors, or income groups in need

new_nodes.label: Multiplier effect amplifies fiscal policy impact
new_nodes.objective: Understand that the multiplier magnifies the output effect of fiscal stimulus.
essentialPoints: Initial change in spending induces further rounds of spending via the multiplier, amplifying the total effect on output

new_nodes.label: Implementation and recognition lags in fiscal policy
new_nodes.objective: Understand how lags reduce the effectiveness of fiscal policy as a stabilisation tool.
essentialPoints: Recognising a downturn and legislating/implementing a fiscal response takes time, so policy may act too slowly

new_nodes.label: Fiscal policy increases public debt and sustainability concerns
new_nodes.objective: Understand the long-run debt cost of expansionary fiscal policy.
essentialPoints: Deficit-financed fiscal expansion adds to public debt, raising future sustainability and interest burden concerns

new_nodes.label: Political constraints and time inconsistency in fiscal policy
new_nodes.objective: Understand how political incentives can distort fiscal policy from optimal stabilisation.
essentialPoints: Elected governments face incentives to time fiscal policy for electoral rather than stabilisation purposes
Difficult to reverse popular spending increases or tax cuts once introduced

issues.explanation: This advantages set has only one node bundling three distinct justifications (speed, independence from political interference, not adding to debt); per the breadth check these should be split, and the disadvantages set is similarly thin/bundled (lags, ZLB, weak transmission, lack of targeting all in one node).

new_nodes.label: Monetary policy can be adjusted quickly
new_nodes.objective: Understand the speed advantage of monetary policy over fiscal policy.
essentialPoints: Central bank committees can change interest rates frequently without needing legislation

new_nodes.label: Central bank independence reduces political interference
new_nodes.objective: Understand how operational independence improves policy credibility.
essentialPoints: Independent central banks are less subject to electoral time-inconsistency problems than elected fiscal policymakers

new_nodes.label: Monetary policy does not directly add to government debt
new_nodes.objective: Understand that monetary expansion avoids the direct fiscal cost of borrowing.
essentialPoints: Changing interest rates or money supply does not require government borrowing or raise public debt directly

new_nodes.label: Ineffectiveness of monetary policy at the zero lower bound
new_nodes.objective: Understand why interest rate cuts cannot stimulate demand once rates are near zero.
essentialPoints: Nominal interest rates cannot easily be cut below zero, limiting further stimulus via conventional tools

new_nodes.label: Weak interest-sensitivity of consumption/investment limits monetary policy
new_nodes.objective: Understand that monetary policy effectiveness depends on the responsiveness of spending to interest rate changes.
essentialPoints: If consumption/investment are not very sensitive to interest rates, monetary policy has limited effect on demand

new_nodes.label: Monetary policy cannot target specific sectors or regions
new_nodes.objective: Understand the lack of precision in monetary policy compared to fiscal tools.
essentialPoints: A single national interest rate affects all sectors/regions uniformly, unlike targeted fiscal measures

issues.explanation: Floating exchange rate advantages set bundles three distinct justifications (automatic trade balance correction, monetary policy autonomy, no reserves needed) in one node - only two nodes exist total for this side, below the 4-6 point breadth expectation.

new_nodes.label: Floating rates free monetary policy for domestic objectives
new_nodes.objective: Understand that a floating regime allows interest rates to target domestic goals rather than defend a peg.
essentialPoints: Without a peg to defend, the central bank can set interest rates to target domestic inflation/output

new_nodes.label: Floating rates avoid the need for large foreign exchange reserves
new_nodes.objective: Understand the reserve-holding cost saved under a floating regime.
essentialPoints: No commitment to defend a fixed rate means no need to hold large reserves for intervention
